There has been some discussion of this matter of "suitable employment," and I would ask the minister to explain the procedure now followed in ascertaining whether the employment offered to a person in receipt of benefits is suitable employment or is not suitable employment, and under what circumstances a person is denied benefit if he does not accept the "suitable employment" offered by the commission.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I have here a brief dealing specially with that, which I might read:
In view of the provisions of the act and the conditions resulting from the war the commission has taken the view that a reasonable interpretation can be made along the following lines:
1.	Where claimants have had technical training and experience in a skilled occupation they should be allowed a considerable period to find work in their own occupation before being required to make a complete change in their occupation and sacrifice their training and experience. The extent of the change of occupation involved would have a bearing on the interval allowed. For certain specified groups of skilled workers, the commission has instructed its offices to allow a period of three months before a change of occupation is insisted upon, provided that employment in the claimant's usual occupation has a place in a peace-time economy and that he is not barred from the occupation by reasons of age, physical deterioration, et cetera.
2.	Occupations which have many of the same characteristics may be segregated into groups. If employment is not available in the claimant's usual occupation he may be offered employment in another occupation in the group in which his usual occupation falls. Because of the similarity of the occupations in this grouping a comparatively short period of unemployment is a reasonable interval.
3.	The extent of the contrast between wages and conditions of work in the usual occupation and the other occupation has a bearing on the period allowed before a change of occupation was insisted upon. The commission does not require claimants imemdiately to accept very much lower rates of wages. However, following the war period the employment available for some of them may use only pre-war skills and may be at lower rates of wages than those to which they have become accustomed during the war. The period allowed for a change of occupation which includes a lower rate is therefore made progres-
Unemployment Insurance

sive. For instance, employment in another occupation at a wage rate of 5 cents an hour lower is considered suitable for some claimants after three weeks of unemployment, while an occupation paying a wage rate of 10 cents an hour lower would be considered suitable only after four weeks of unemployment.
4.	Other factors taken into account by the commission are the number of years the claimant has been employed in his usual occupation, provided it is a skilled occupation; distance of work offered from the claimant's home; prospect's of work in his own occupation, either in his own district or in another district; domestic responsibilities of the claimant and adaptability of the claimant, particularly where employment is in another part of the country.
5.	Workers discharged from purely war work in plants, for example, shell-filling plants, where there are few if any similar skills required in peace-time industry, may be offered employment in another occupation with practically no interval allowed.
6.	Persons who have been transferred from one part of the country to another to engage in war industry and who choose to return to the areas in which they formerly resided, may reasonably be expected to accept any work available in those areas without any interval.
7.	Workers trained in specific war jobs with previous experience in some other occupation should be allowed only a short interval before being required to accept employment in an occupation in which they have had some experience.
Ini addition to that, we have set up across the country courts of referees composed of a chairman and representatives pf the trade union and employers, and from these courts of referees there is a further appeal to the umpire. Probably my hon. friends have had more complaints than I have, but as a rule any complaints that are made funnel into the minister's office and those I have received up to now have been few and far between. In Great Britain they have had the same difficulty with much longer experience than we have had. We are just moving into what might be called the administrative period in the application of unemployment insurance. With the end of the war and the reconversion of industry, a measure of unemployment in any country that was engaged in the war-any free country at least-is inevitable, and in Great Britain they have had a measure of unemployment. To-day there are between four hundred thousand and five hundred thousand people registered for unemployment insurance, notwithstanding the fact that there the labour situation is much tighter than in Canada. I would assume that, in the light of the experience gained by the courts of referees and by the umpire, we shall be able to build up a system of precedents that will permit the orderly administration of this difficult aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Frankly, I do not believe that we have had enough experience because in this country this is a virgin field of a kind that does not exist

in Great Britain, where they have not the same seasonal employments that we have in the dominion. However, I think it can be stated that the courts of referees, the insurance officers, and the umpire will, in the course of the day-by-day application of this vital and difficult aspect of the administration of this measure, build up a method of procedure which, in the light of experience, will meet the situation in Canada. We have at the moment seven thousand cases before boards of referees.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: The act provides for the training of persons who have lost employment, in order to fit them for other work. subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: That problem has not been a difficult one up to now. Of course we have thousands of veterans in training under the jurisdiction of my department. We have not so many civilian war workers. One of the most amazing things is this. At the collapse of Japan I had jurisdiction over the selection, and power of direction, of the men and women in the industrial and agricultural life of the country. I came to the conclusion, against the advice of many people, that the quicker we got rid of these controls, the better it would be for Canada, and in about four months we put more than a million people, through the employment service, into the employment stream of Canada, which is an indication- if we get suitable labour relations-of the ability of this country to face up to the problems of peace and a measure of full employment. Of course we are interfered with by conditions in other countries. The coal strike in the United States, and more particularly the steel strike, had a great impact upon employment conditions in Canada. But we expect, should the need arise, to be able to expand the application of the training of war workers in vocations necessary to fit them into the industrial and commercial life of the country. The pressure, however, has not been great up to now.

We started off with a much larger coverage than that. In commencing their scheme in Great Britain, they were fortunate in that there was comparatively full employment. We were fortunate in Canada in that we were able to build up a fund because there was comparatively full employment in this country. In Great Britain, where they have social cohesion and climatic conditions somewhat different from what they are in Canada, where employment in farming is more or less looked upon as a trade or calling, it was twenty-five years after the inception of the plan in that country before agriculture was brought within the orbit of unemployment insurance. I hope it will not take twenty-five years for us to do it in Canada, particularly in my hon. friend's province where climatic conditions beyond the coastal range are similar to what they are in Great Britain and in New Zealand, in that there are not the great extremes of climate which we have in eastern Canada. In the light of the length of time since the inception of the plan in Canada the tempo of movement in the coverage under the act has been far greater than in any other country that I know of. After the insurance officer has made his decision, the employee has the right [DOT] to go before a board of referees composed of an equal representation of labour and management with an impartial chairman. In my experience I have found that if you have a good case you need have no fear of going before a tribunal of that description. If employees do not get from the board of referees what they consider to be justice they still have the right to appeal to the umpire. I do not think I can say much more than that. I am a great believer in the system of adjudicating disputes. We would have less trouble in the industrial field to-day if the orgainzations we set up, composed of employees and employers, were given the respect to which they are entitled by people who ask for representation on these boards or commissions or whatever the case may be.

But I think we as a parliament must be vigilant in these things because, as my hon. friends to my right are so careful to point out on every possible occasion, bureau-

cratic boards may get into the habit of ordering people around. Consequently we have to be on guard here and, if there is any need for criticism, we should offer that criticism as a guide and suggestions to those boards. That is the way in which I approach the matter. I do not for one moment doubt the sincerity and the desire of the unemployment insurance commission to administer this act fairly and efficiently. I have had some correspondence with them. I have also held conversation with them, and I am convinced on that point.
But in this circular 34 there is an item which the minister did not read. I should imagine he has not read it all, and I am not suggesting that his not having read it is any indication that he has tried to hold anything back. Section 11 at page 3 of the copy I have states:
If an applicant is seeking employment in an occupation which is no longer found in his locality, he must be prepared to change his residence if he still desires work in that occupation.
What help is given a person under these circumstances who may have to move from one locality to another? He may be put off unemployment insurance benefits, and move to another area.

Unemployment Insurance

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Speaking of robbing the bank, I believe there are some instances where unemployment insurance has been taken advantage of by the very people whom it is intended to benefit. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a case which recently came to my notice. This man owned or operated a farm and, after hostilities commenced, he obtained employment in war work. Vt that time he made over his farm to his wife without any consideration and she continued to look after the farming operation. When the war ended, his employment with the company he had been working with ceased. He has since been working on the farm, which is owned by his wife, during the daytime, and after six o'clock he goes to work as an electrician. During this period he has been drawing unemployment insurance at the rate of S14.40 a week.
I am informed that he is able to do this because he is actually working in the day time on a farm. When he went to fill in the form he stated that he was working on the farm during the daytime when actually he is working also as an electrician after six o'clock at night. I will not say that he has been getting away with something, but the fact is he is getting $14.40 a week when he is working on a farm in the daytime and continuing his employment as electrician at night. This man does not think he is doing anything wrong, because the advertisements and notices that have gone out from the employment service have led him to believe that he has a credit of so many dollars and he thinks he has a right to draw on that. I think loopholes of this sort should be sealed up and the regulations redrawn and the forms prepared in such a manner that this sort of thing cannot happen.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: I would think that individual had made a false declaration and, if my hon. friend will give me the name privately, I shall be glad to have the commission look into the matter. Under the act as it stands, at the moment a person is entitled to earn $1 a day as subsidiary earnings, but if this farmer-electrician is holding down two jobs I should like to know who he is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I wish to make one more appeal to the minister to take up with the people who had to do with the drafting of this memorandum the matter of having it discarded or at least rewritten. I grant that there are some things in it that have to be there for the purposes of administration, but the tone of it has got under the skin of a good many trade union people. The minister replied to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East in connection with a man 
seeking employment in an occupation which no longer offers employment in his own locality, by stating that the fares of people who move were paid. It is one thing to be willing to pay the fare of a person who wants to move, but is another thing to give the impression that a person must move or he will forfeit a right which he thinks he has because of having paid into a fund. There is another section a little further along in this bulletin No. 34, which reads:
For example, it may not be expedient during the early days of unemployment to require him to take work in another district, but as the hopes of obtaining suitable employment in his home district diminish, work at a distance may have to be regarded as suitable.
It may be that something like that has to be included for the purposes of administration, but the minister knows as well as I that statements such as that have an effect upon working conditions and wage levels. I think I speak for all of us who have been objecting to this memorandum from this side of the house when I say that we do not rise to express the view that there is in this instance any need of a fundamental change in the Unemployment Insurance Act, but that the government should realize the wider implications and be on its guard against being responsible for the depressing of wage levels.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to bring to the attention of the commission the observations of my hon. friends in connection with this document. I would point out that Canada is a continent, not a country. In a vast country like this you must have a measure of mobility of labour. At the present time I am moving people from Nova Scotia into the Maine woods. We are expecting to move farmers from western Canada to the east and eastern farmers to the west in order to get off the harvest. The hon. member for Vancouver East will remember that last fall we received an appeal from the city council about the congregation of labour in Vancouver, and at that time we considered it necessary that we render a measure of assistance to that municipality by providing for the migration back to where they came from of that labour which had come to that district for purely war industry purposes.
These things are not static; they are active. We must make every effort, to place these people in gainful employment. My hon. friend has often spoken of conditions in Great Britain. After the previous war they had in South Wales and other districts, particularly in Barrow, what were referred to as depressed areas, and efforts were made to move labour from Barrow into other parts of the country.

Unemployment Insurance
In a country like Canada, with 12,000,000 people squatting on a continent, we cannot take the position where we can say, "Hamilton and no further", or Regina or Moose Jaw or what have you. I do not know how we could expect to make this country tick under those conditions. By the very nature of things we are bound to have stagnation in certain industries. An example of this was the aeroplane industry after the end of the war. It is necessary to provide for the movement of labour to other parts of the country where gainful employment can be found.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: I concur in the statement of the minister about providing for the mobility of labour, but what we are talking about is using language in connection with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act to the effect that people must be prepared to move. It is the "must" we do not like.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I received a letter from a man in Montreal which I should like to read, and then I will ask the Minister of Labour his opinion of it. This letter is signed "John C. Wilson" and is headed, "A new serfdom." It reads:
Do the veterans realize the shameless swindle which is to be put over them under the guise or mask of unemployment insurance? The correspondence columns of the Montreal papers should be read throughout Canada. In response to several complaints ("Jobless for four months, and not received a cent," et cetera, et cetera) the actual facts have been stated with admirable clearness in Montreal Daily Star of May 13 on page 3 by the assistant manager, Mr. Heffernan.
He quotes this by Mr. Heffernan:
"Unless the job is accepted, the man will be disqualified from benefits for six weeks." Whatever his skill or qualifications, whether skilled mechanic or white-collar worker, ''as long as the pay is within the minimum set by the province of Quebec, even if as an unskilled furniture-worker at 20 cents an hour, he will be disqualified."
Not only so. "Every refusal thereafter, even during the six weeks, will add a similar period to his disqualification." Thus a skilled tradesman or even an accountant or professional man, who persistently refuses work at 20 cents an hour, will never receive a cent of unemployment insurance.
If the proper English word for this is not "peonage," what is the correct word for it?

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will let me have the letter I shall be glad to look into it. I am sure that he cannot ask me, with about 2,300,000 people insured under this scheme, to know them all. But I shall be glad to look into it.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
But is it the fact, that highly skilled men will be forced to take any unskilled! job?
Mr, MITCHELL: The answer to that is, no.

An insured person shall be deemed not to be unemployed . . .
And then it goes on-

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS

In the drafting of a bill like this, and the amendments, I w'ant to be very frank in saying that the recommendations come at a period when we do not feel it advisable, particularly in the light of economic conditions at the moment, that the amendment should be made this year.

That statement surprises me, because I had understood that another class was to be added to the classes of payments which would be a class at a higher rate and would make higher contributions and would receive higher benefits. If human nature follows the trend indicated after the last war, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said to-day, we may be in a very difficult position on the North American continent a year from now. speechtext: May I suggest that the minister stick to labour.

I have the floor at the moment, and I do not wish to get into an argument on phony money at this moment any more than anyone else wants to argue about it just now. I have expressed my opinion and my hon. friends can express theirs. Let me say that the reason why we are moving with caution in the extension of coverage in respect of all these things is that we do not know what the relation will be a year from now between the present value of the dollar and the value of the dollar as it was in 1940, 1941, 1942 and 1943. No one can make any such prediction in view of what has happened in the United States in the last couple of weeks. They may be moving into an inflationary spiral with the inevitable collapse afterwards. We are living in peculiar times, and all I can say is that I trust that at this time next year conditions will be more stable than they are at the moment.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I had naturally thought, from what I have heard the minister say with regard to the government's price control policy and their ability to handle the situation, that the much feared deflation after inflation would not ensue. Apparently the minister is not so sure now when he comes to this point. Would he tell us whether or not the report of the advisory committee on these possible increases of rates and benefits took into consideration the uncertain state of financial affairs in the world? If the advisory committee have taken that question into consideration, then surely, they being concerned more than anyone else with the actuarial basis of the fund, their recommendation would be a safe one for the government to follow. It seems to me that there are already increases in the cost of various articles. If, therefore, these possible increases are withheld it will be a serious matter.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I wonder if the advisory committee has given some thought to increasing the differential between the rate for a single person or a person without dependents and the rate for a person with dependents. If you look at these rates you will find that apparently it does not cost very much for a man to keep his wife, or vice versa, for the wife who is working to keep her husband. If a single man or woman is unemployed in category 2 the rate is $5.10 a week. If a married person, male or female, with a dependent is unemployed that person receives ninety cents extra, which brings it to $6. These rates that were set out in 1940 when the bill was passed should be revised upwards at least to the extent that the cost of living has gone up and to the extent that we feel it will go up within the next few months, though, of course, I realize that you cannot keep moving a scale of benefits of this kind up and down as the cost of living rises or falls a few points. The differential, however, is far too small, and I suggest that the advisory committee give thought to increasing it as between the person without dependents and the person with dependents. The minister will remember, as those of us who dealt with this matter a few years ago remember, that, following the last war, in Great Britain a substantial fund had been laid aside, but it was not very long until the whole fund running into hundreds of millions of dollars had been dissipated. I do not mean that the money had been wasted, but it had been drawn out because of the great amount of unemployment.
We might run up against the same condition in this country, and it must not be taken as a reflection upon the Unemployment Insurance Act. The whole purpose of the fund is good. But both employers and employees will have to use their heads and meet situations as they arise. I am one who believes that if such a time should come we should be ready with the finances of the country to support it. The fund, which so many people seem to think is large, may actually be too small. But if such a time should come support should be given sufficient to carry on the obligations under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I have great faith in it. It has done a wonderful job, both in the old country and in Canada, as long as we have had it. It must
not be allowed to fail. The country itself, through its finances, would have to save the fund if and when it became depleted, to that extent.

There is another matter I should like to bring up. Representations have been made to me by certain employees of the city of Vancouver who have been removed from the act. These employees work in the cemeteries which are owned by the city. I took the matter up with the chief commissioner, and he sent me the following letter under date of June 5, 1946:
I might explain that insurability of employment by cemeteries came up for consideration a couple of years ago when it was drawn to the attention of this commission that an anomaly

existed which had given rise to some grievance. As you know, many cemeteries are operated by churches and other bodies which are classed as charitable institutions within the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance Act. These institutions are not required to insure their employees and this exception extends to employees of cemeteries operated by them.
On the other hand, cemeteries operated by municipalities and by private companies were required to insure their employees. Strong objection was taken by some of the latter and representations were made to the commissioner to remove the anomaly by exercising the powers granted under section 14 (1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which reads as follows:
After quoting the section, which I do not think I will read since the minister will have it before him, the letter continues:
As a result the commission made a regulation, which came into effect on April 22, 1944, which was the item quoted in the letter of April 9 from the accountant for Vancouver. The regulation provides in effect that any cemetery which is required to furnish graves to the poor without charge is relieved from making contributions for its employees. The provincial statutes of most of the provinces require both municipal and private cemeteries to do so and for this reason they felt that they should be put on the same basis as charitable institutions.
The cemeteries in the city of Vancouver are not charitable institutions; they are run by the city. A person employed to-day by the cemetery department may be employed tomorrow by some other department. These employees want to come under the Unemployment Insurance Act so that they may draw benefits if unemployed. They feel that if employees of charitable institutions are exempt there is no reason why they should be. As employees of the city I think they have as much right to be covered by the act as employees of any other department of the city.

Privately owned power plants came under the act, while municipal and provincial power plants were exempted, and they were all put under the act.

What additional duties are to be given to the commission? Subsection 4 of the new section 88 reads:
The commission shall assume and carry out such other duties and responsibilities -as the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, may require from time to time and, in respect of such other duties and responsibilities, shall be responsible to the minister.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
Speaking now as an individual, I want to say that I believe in ministerial responsibility. During the war we had to use the employment service for many things which were not covered by the legislation but which had to be done by order in council. At the present moment we are doing many things through the instrumentality of the employment service that are not covered by legislation. One item is apprenticeship training. For registration and all things necessary to carry this out in the different provinces we use the employment service. In the training of veterans we use the employment service; I mean that they move through that organization. Sometimes it is necessary to take a strike vote in some industry, and I use the agency for that purpose. Or take the movement of farm labour during the war, when we moved hundreds of thousands of people from agriculture in the winter to the other basic industries in the country; that was done under the direction of the minister through the employment service. I regard the employment service as a dynamic institution. You have to be prepared to make decisions, make them quickly, and give the necessary direction. I believe it can be truthfully said, notwithstanding some criticism, that without the employment service and the direction given to it by or through the minister during the war period, we would have had a very difficult situation in this country. Had we not had an employment service at the close of the war where, through ministerial responsibility, we could act quickly and
give the necessary direction from day to day, I do not believe we would have passed through these last six or seven months as we have done. My mind goes back to the last war, when only ten per cent of the industrial structure of this nation was engaged in war production.
That, in short, is the story. I cannot tell what to-morrow I may find it necessary that the employment service should do under the direction of the minister. My hon. friend can rest assured that anything which should be done will be done through the medium of that organization, if it is in the interests of the economic well-being of this nation, of the employers and of the working people who go to make up its working force.

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext: The idea is that there shall be wide power given to the employment service for these special duties?

speechtext: We had that power, of course, under the national selective service. It is in effect. What we want to get is a running picture from day to day of the employment situation in Canada. speechtext: Does the minister think it will be possible to get every person who is looking for a job first to report that fact to the employment service? I suggest to the minister that there is no need to go that far. I appreciate fully the import of what my hon. friend says. One reason I took the course of eliminating the controls in selective service was the very simple reason my hon. friend has just enunciated. I thought there would be such a tremendous movement of labour that our offices would not be able to handle it, that we would have congregations of people in downtown Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto and so on. Some of my officials warned me against the sudden dropping of these controls, but I said to them, "You will be amazed at what free men can do, how they will find a niche for themselves in the economy of this country." I believe our decision has been justified by what has happened since then. As I have said, over a million people were put into the


Unemployment Insurance
employment stream in the course of four months without any undue stress or strain on the employment service.
What I am driving at here, however, is merely a reporting system. I do not want people to go to employment offices, but we want to know the ebb and flow, the turnover in the labour market of this country. This may be a jump in the dark. It may be the wrong thing to do, but we feel that we can have a more reliable barometer of employment conditions by applying this very simple idea of reporting both by the employer and the employee, who, however, does not have to go to the employment office.

speechtext:
Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of bill No. 127, to amend the Public Printing and Stationery Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Repeal.

maintopic: REPEAL OF PROVISION OF ACT RESPECTING DUTIES OF CLERK OF PRINTING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the Secretary of State jive us an explanation?

maintopic: REPEAL OF PROVISION OF ACT RESPECTING DUTIES OF CLERK OF PRINTING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Section 3 of the Public Printing and Stationery Act which it is intended to repeal was passed during the session of 1888. It will be seen that the
TMr. Mitchell.]
committee referred to in section 3 was therein empowered to employ a clerk independent of the authorities of the houses of parliament. The chairman of the joint committee on printing chose the job printing companies which were to handle the tvork and the clerk of the committee acting as his secretary had equal power. Section 3 of the Printing and Stationery Act is now obsolete, because the staffs of the Senate and the House of Commons have been reorganized, and their permanent officers, clerks and employees are appointed under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Moreover, the committee has now no right to make appointments. Standing order 82 states that the Clerk has direction and control over all the officers and clerks employed in the offices subject to such orders as he may from time to time receive from Mr. Speaker or from parliament itself. According to section 3, ivliich it is proposed to repeal, the chairman of the committee can theoretically ignore the Speaker and the Clerk of the house and give whatever orders he desires. Obviously it is desirable that this conflict should not exist, and that this obsolete section should be removed. That is the purpose of the measure.

speechtext:
Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of bill No. 125, to amend the House of Commons Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Repeal.

subtopic: REPEAL OF PROVISIONS NOW SUPERSEDED BY CONSOLIDATED REVENUE AND AUDIT ACT
speechtext: Will the minister explain the purpose of this bill?

subtopic: REPEAL OF PROVISIONS NOW SUPERSEDED BY CONSOLIDATED REVENUE AND AUDIT ACT
speechtext:
It is to remove from the operative sections of existing statutes certain obsolete clauses. Prior to 1931 there was no provision in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act for issuing moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund for the administrative expenditures of the House of Commons. Letters of credit signed by the Speaker and two commissioners of internal economy of the house were periodically sent to the treasury for amounts required during a certain period, usually three months. The letter of credit was issued in favour of the accountant of the house who had been duly authorized to receive it by the Speaker.

United Nations
In the revision of the Audit Act, during the session of 1931, the words "public moneys" were defined so as to include all revenue from any source whatsoever, and section 3 declares that all public moneys shall form the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Section 27 of the revised act provides that all issue of public moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund shall be made under the direction of the comptroller by cheque. The procedure is laid out in regulations and other sections of the act. These cover the issue of moneys required for the House of Commons; and therefore sections 19 and 20 of the House of Commons Act, which it is intended to repeal under this bill, have not been used since 1931, are obsolete and useless and should be deleted from our statutes.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed. EXPORT CREDITS INSURANCE ACT
